content_html:
A health savings account (HSA) is a tax-advantaged account for medical costs, available to people covered by a high-deductible health plan (HDHP). It is the only US account with three tax breaks: contributions are deductible or come out of pay before tax, the balance can be invested and grow tax-free, and withdrawals for qualified medical expenses are never taxed. This calculator projects your HSA balance, the tax you save, and how medical spending along the way affects what is left.

How to use this calculator

  1. HDHP coverage and age: these set your contribution limit. Family coverage has a higher limit, and from age 55 you can add a catch-up contribution.
  2. Current balance and years to project: where you start and how far ahead to look.
  3. Your contribution and employer contribution: both count toward the same annual limit. Tick "Contribute the maximum" to fill whatever room the employer leaves.
  4. Medical expenses paid from the HSA: your yearly qualified costs that you plan to pay from the account. The amount rises each year by the rate under More options.
  5. Expected annual return: what the invested balance earns. Cash left in an HSA's default savings option often earns much less than an investment fund.
  6. Tax rates and payroll: used to estimate the tax you save on your own contributions. Contributions through an employer's payroll also avoid Social Security and Medicare tax.

2026 HSA limits

ItemSelf-onlyFamily
Contribution limit (you plus employer)$4,400$8,750
Extra catch-up at age 55 or older$1,000$1,000
Minimum HDHP deductible$1,700$3,400
Maximum HDHP out-of-pocket costs$8,500$17,000

The catch-up belongs to each account holder, so a married couple who are both 55 or older need two HSAs to use both catch-ups. The projection holds these limits at their 2026 levels for every future year.

How the projection works

At the start of each year, your contribution and your employer's are added, capped at the limit for your coverage and age. That year's medical expenses are then paid from the account, but never more than the balance; anything above it is flagged as paid from other money. The remaining balance grows by the expected return. Tax saved is your own contribution multiplied by your federal and state rates, plus 7.65% for Social Security and Medicare tax when you contribute through payroll.

Worked example

A 35-year-old with self-only coverage and $2,000 in an HSA puts in $3,400 a year, and their employer adds $500. They pay $1,000 a year of medical costs from the account, rising 3% a year, and invest the rest at 5%. Their tax rates are 22% federal and 5% state, and they contribute through payroll.

  • Balance at 65: $181,240.
  • Contributions total $117,000 and $47,575 goes to medical bills along the way, while investment growth adds $109,816.
  • Their own contributions save about $1,178 of tax a year, or $35,343 over 30 years.

If they paid those medical bills from other money and left the HSA invested, the balance at 65 would be about $280,711.

Tips for getting the most from an HSA

  • Keep receipts. There is no deadline for reimbursing yourself for a qualified expense incurred after the HSA was opened, so you can pay bills now and withdraw the money tax-free years later.
  • After 65, withdrawals for anything other than medical costs are taxed as income but no longer owe the 20% additional tax, so the account works much like a traditional IRA.
  • Medicare premiums (except Medigap) and long-term care insurance premiums, within limits, are qualified expenses.
  • Stop contributing once you enroll in any part of Medicare. Premium-free Part A can be backdated up to six months when you sign up after 65, so many people stop contributions earlier.

faq.question: What is the HSA contribution limit for 2026?
faq.answer: For 2026 the limit is $4,400 with self-only HDHP coverage and $8,750 with family coverage. Account holders who are 55 or older by the end of the year can add $1,000. Employer contributions count toward these limits.

faq.question: Who can contribute to an HSA?
faq.answer: You need to be covered by a qualifying high-deductible health plan, have no other disqualifying health coverage, not be enrolled in Medicare and not be claimed as a dependent on someone else's return. For 2026, an HDHP must have a deductible of at least $1,700 for self-only or $3,400 for family coverage. Starting in 2026, bronze and catastrophic plans offered as individual coverage on a health insurance Exchange also count as HSA-eligible, even if they don't meet those deductible and out-of-pocket rules.

faq.question: What happens to my HSA if I change jobs or health plans?
faq.answer: The account is yours. Unlike a flexible spending account, the balance never expires and stays with you when you change jobs or plans. You can keep spending it on qualified medical costs even if you no longer have an HDHP, though you can't add new money without one.

faq.question: What if I use HSA money for something that isn't medical?
faq.answer: Before 65, a non-medical withdrawal is taxed as income and also owes a 20% additional tax. From 65, or if you become disabled, the 20% tax no longer applies, but the withdrawal is still taxed as income.

faq.question: Should I invest my HSA or keep it in cash?
faq.answer: Many people keep enough cash to cover their deductible and invest the rest for long-term growth. Investments can lose value, so money you expect to spend soon is usually better kept in cash.
